snippet.title: Why Your Water Heater Should Be a Battery
snippet.description:
How This Heat Pump Water Heater is Also a Battery. Go to https://ground.news/undecided for an innovative way to stay fully informed on tech, energy, the climate and more. Save 40% on the Ground News unlimited access Vantage plan with my link. Heat pump water heaters have been around for over a decade. If you follow this channel, you probably know they're three to five times more efficient than a standard electric tank. Maybe you've got one. I do. But here's what most people don't realize. Even if you own a heat pump water heater, it's still pretty dumb. It heats reactively. The tank drops below the setpoint, the compressor kicks on. It doesn't know your schedule. It doesn't know your electricity rates. And it definitely doesn't know when your solar panels are cranking. Two Boston startups think that's a massive missed opportunity. They're treating the water heater as a thermal battery, a cheap, insulated vessel that can store energy as heat, shift electricity use to cheaper hours, and participate in grid services. One of them, Wilmington, Massachusetts-based Cala Systems, invited me to tour their factory. Their predictive software is licensed from the National Renewable Energy Lab. According to a California Energy Commission study, intelligent scheduling on time-of-use rate plans alone can cut costs by 15 to 19 percent beyond what a standard heat pump water heater already saves. So I went inside to find out: is a smart water heater actually worth the premium? Or is "intelligent" just a buzzword bumper sticker slapped on a tank of hot water?

Wi-Fi / “always online”

Cala does not rely on an internet connection to function - the core controls run on the unit itself. Connecting to Wi-Fi enables additional functionality like software updates, remote diagnostic support, app control, and heating coordination with solar, electricity pricing, and more.

Security / Remote Access 
Remote diagnostics are opt-in - if you keep the unit offline, no data is shared. If you do connect, all sent data is encrypted and enables our technical team to more quickly detect, diagnose, and resolve any potential issues. There is no subscription and no fee for this functionality!

Can a 12V 100Ah LiFePO4 battery survive repeated heavy-load testing and then handle a 250A+ overcurrent test?

In this review, I put the Dumfume 12V 100Ah battery through a test sequence that goes beyond a normal capacity test.

First, I run my “BB Test”: three separate 50A discharge tests in a row. This is the same style of repeated-load testing that exposed problems with a major-brand battery in earlier testing.

Then I push the battery even harder with a 250A+ overcurrent test to see how the BMS responds, whether the battery shuts down correctly, and whether there are signs of excessive heat, instability, or damage.

A battery can look great on paper. The real question is what happens after repeated demand, then a serious overcurrent event.

⚡ WHAT I TEST

* Dumfume 12V 100Ah LiFePO4 battery
* Three consecutive 50A discharge tests
* My repeated-load “BB Test”
* Battery behavior between test cycles
* Voltage under load
* Temperature and heat concerns
* BMS protection behavior
* 250A+ overcurrent test
* Recovery after overcurrent protection
* Capacity and real-world performance
* Whether it makes sense for RV, solar, backup, or portable power use

🔋 WHY THREE BACK-TO-BACK 50A TESTS MATTER

A single discharge test does not always tell the whole story.

Some batteries may appear fine during the first heavy load, then show problems after repeated cycles. That can reveal weak connections, BMS issues, heat buildup, voltage instability, or poor recovery after stress.

The three consecutive 50A tests are designed to see whether the battery can continue performing after it has already been pushed hard.

I am watching for:

* Voltage sag
* Heat buildup
* Early shutdown
* BMS instability
* Slow recovery
* Terminal or cable heat
* Reduced performance between cycles
* Any sign that the battery is not handling repeated demand well

⚠️ THE 250A+ OVERCURRENT TEST

After the repeated 50A testing, I push the battery into a 250A+ overcurrent condition.

The goal is not to abuse equipment for no reason. The goal is to see whether the battery’s protection system responds as expected when demand exceeds what the battery should safely provide.

For a high-current test like this, I am watching for:

* Proper BMS shutdown behavior
* Safe recovery after protection trips
* Excessive heat
* Voltage instability
* Damage or warning signs
* Whether the battery behaves predictably after the test

snippet.title: Live: Top 10 Hurricane Prep Mistakes Solar Owners Make
snippet.description:
Hurricane season is here, and a lot of solar owners may not be nearly as ready as they think.

In this livestream, we are going through the Top 10 Hurricane Prep Mistakes Solar Owners Make — from assuming rooftop solar works during a grid outage, to not having battery backup, no transfer switch, no critical-load plan, no fuel plan, and not testing the system before the storm is already on the way.

Most rooftop solar systems are grid-tied, and many still do not include battery backup. Wood Mackenzie reported that the U.S. residential solar-plus-storage attachment rate reached 25% in Q1 2024, which means roughly 75% of new residential solar installs at that time were still solar-only. If the grid goes down, many of those systems will shut down unless they are designed with backup power in mind.

Tonight we’ll talk about:
• Why solar panels alone may not power your house during an outage
• The biggest battery backup mistakes
• Generator vs battery backup planning
• Critical loads and what you really need to keep running
• Transfer switches, interlocks, and safe power transfer
• Internet, communications, and monitoring during outages
• Spare parts, extension cords, fuel, and storm timing
• What I would do differently before a hurricane

This livestream is meant to help homeowners, DIY solar users, RV owners, and anyone thinking about backup power build a safer and more realistic storm plan.

Next week we’ll continue the conversation with a roundtable livestream featuring other YouTubers talking about their disaster recovery plans, solar backup systems, storm prep, and how they would handle hurricanes, tornadoes, floods, snowstorms, and long-term outages.
